feed.title: Wits AHEAD · Daily briefing
feed.subtitle: News, research, video and readings on AI, data and human capability in higher education, curated every morning.
feed.rights: Wits AHEAD Research Group, Wits School of Education, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: WISE and Education Collaborative partner with five African universities on an AI adoption pilot
entry.summary:
WISE, the World Innovation Summit for Education, and Ashesi University's Education Collaborative have launched an AI adoption pilot with five African universities: Bells University of Technology in Nigeria, Botho University in Botswana, KCA University in Kenya, the University of Kigali in Rwanda and Université d'Abomey-Calavi in Benin. Running from October 2026 to June 2027, each university is trialling a project suited to its own priorities, from curriculum-aligned AI tutors and adaptive learning tools to early-warning systems and institutional governance frameworks. The pilot builds on a 2025 baseline study of 47 African universities, which found AI adoption fragmented and governance thin.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on responsible AI governance, this is a rare multi-country trial that tests AI tools and institutional policy together across five very different African universities, offering early comparative evidence of what responsible adoption looks like in practice.

africa.com (WISE and The Education Collaborative, Ashesi University) · International education initiative announcement

entry.title: Early success indicators at a South African university: a data-centric approach to student success
entry.summary:
Philokuhle Majozi and Kgadi Mathabathe of the University of Pretoria have proposed an “early success indicators” framework that maps data points and support interventions across the whole student lifecycle, from before registration through to final assessment. Drawing on interviews with academic success coaches, institutional leaders and data scientists, the framework favours a strengths-based, proactive model over deficit-oriented “at-risk” early-warning systems.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This gives Wits AHEAD's predictive-analytics pillar a South African, strengths-based alternative to conventional early-warning models, directly relevant to designing retention interventions that support rather than merely flag struggling students.

Journal of Student Affairs in Africa · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Cambridge-led OpRaise report: AI markers favour style over substance in university essays
entry.summary:
Researchers from the Universities of Cambridge, Manchester Metropolitan and Nottingham tested three leading AI models, singly and in combination, on 761 undergraduate psychology essays from three UK universities. The models agreed closely with each other but less with human examiners, consistently rewarding longer, more complex writing regardless of academic merit and compressing marks toward the middle of the scale.

Why it matters for AHEAD: As Wits AHEAD weighs AI's role in assessment, this is rigorous, multi-institution evidence that automated marking still favours style over substance, a caution against replacing human judgement in Global South universities with far larger classes and fewer markers.

University of Cambridge, Manchester Metropolitan University and the University of Nottingham (OpRaise project) · University research report

entry.title: World Bank video: Korea Partnership Facility forum explores AI for education and skills
entry.summary:
The World Bank Group's YouTube channel has published a short film on this year's Korea-World Bank Group Partnership Facility forum, where officials from Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance, World Bank specialists and a KAIST professor discussed how artificial intelligence can strengthen learning and prepare people for the jobs of the future. The Facility funds AI and digital programmes for education and skills systems in developing countries.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Pillar 4, it shows that international financial institutions now treat AI skills training as central to graduate employability and just transitions, not an add-on.

World Bank Group (YouTube) · International financial institution, official video channel

entry.title: Study finds South African universities' AI policies strong on student rules, thin on privacy and staff duties
entry.summary:
A qualitative study of the generative AI guidelines published by South African public universities finds that only 46 per cent of institutions had an institution-wide policy at the time of the analysis. Where guidelines existed, they set out detailed rules on transparency and student accountability, but covered privacy, data governance and staff accountability only briefly and mostly as advice rather than binding rules.

Why it matters for AHEAD: It is squarely Pillar 6 evidence for Wits AHEAD: the authors call for harmonised, privacy by design AI guidance across the sector, which is exactly the responsible AI gap the group tracks.

Universal Access in the Information Society · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Smartphone AI tools help STEM teachers in low-resource African classrooms move beyond chalk and talk, study finds
entry.summary:
A Universiti Sains Malaysia-led case study worked with ten STEM teachers from Nigeria, Botswana, Ghana, Namibia and Sierra Leone in a hands-on workshop using AI speech-to-image tools, smartphone block coding and circuit simulation. The teachers said the tools made abstract science concepts easier to show, let learners without laptops build coding skills on a smartphone, and let them test circuits safely before touching scarce real equipment.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Pillar 3, it is good evidence that carefully chosen, low-cost AI tools, not expensive hardware, are what can move STEM teaching in under-resourced African classrooms from chalk and talk to real inquiry.

ECNU Review of Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Africa must build its own AI and data, not just adopt it, UFS tells QS Africa Forum
entry.summary:
At the QS Africa Forum 2026 in Addis Ababa, Professor Sam Tshehla, Deputy Vice-Chancellor at the University of the Free State, told the session on the AI imperative and the future of higher education that African universities must move beyond reacting to artificial intelligence and build their own datasets and systems that reflect the continent's languages, cultures and development priorities. He said AI can support the whole student lifecycle, from admissions to teaching and research, but only with investment in digital literacy, governance and ethical frameworks.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Pillar 6's work on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the call for African-owned data and systems matches Wits AHEAD's own emphasis on locally grounded, rather than imported, approaches to AI governance in the Global South.

University of the Free State · University report

entry.title: AI exposure linked to 13 percentage point rise in top grades, Berkeley working paper finds
entry.summary:
A working paper by Igor Chirikov of the Center for Studies in Higher Education at the University of California, Berkeley, analysed more than 500,000 grades from 2018 to 2025 at a large research university. In courses with more writing and coding tasks, the share of A grades rose by 13 percentage points after the release of ChatGPT, about 30 per cent above the 2022 baseline, with the largest increases where take-home work counted most towards the final mark.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Pillar 1's work on generative AI in teaching, assessment and integrity, the study is a caution against reading rising grades as better learning: Wits AHEAD's assessment redesign work needs to weigh homework-heavy and take-home tasks against this same risk.

Center for Studies in Higher Education, UC Berkeley · Working paper, University of California, Berkeley (CSHE)

entry.title: Generative AI closes three-quarters of the productivity gap between more and less educated workers, NBER study finds
entry.summary:
A National Bureau of Economic Research working paper by Guillermo Cruces, Diego Fernández Meijide, Sebastian Galiani, Ramiro H. Gálvez and María Lombardi reports a randomised experiment with 1,174 adults completing a business problem-solving task. Without generative AI, participants with higher education outperformed those with less education by 0.548 standard deviations; with AI assistance, that gap fell to 0.139 standard deviations, closing about three-quarters of the original difference. The advantage held only partly once the AI tool was removed for a follow-up task.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 4 work on graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the finding is double-edged: generative AI can narrow long-standing gaps in task performance, but the advantage fades without sustained effort, so curricula must still build the underlying capability that AI only assists.

National Bureau of Economic Research · Working paper, National Bureau of Economic Research

entry.title: World Bank warns AI's benefits in Africa could bypass the poorest households
entry.summary:
The World Bank's Africa Economic Update for October 2026, titled 'Building AI Readiness', projects economic growth in Sub-Saharan Africa rising from 4.1 per cent in 2025 to 4.3 per cent in 2026, with developer activity climbing fast: Nigeria's community of software developers on GitHub has grown tenfold since 2020, and Ghana's nearly eightfold. The report argues that artificial intelligence could lift productivity and create jobs across the region, but says adoption remains uneven and concentrated in a few economies, chiefly Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa. It names reliable electricity, affordable connectivity, digital skills and public sector capacity as conditions still missing in much of the region.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 6 work on responsible AI, equity and policy, the report is a clear caution that higher education systems across the Global South cannot assume AI's benefits will arrive on their own; building the basic digital and institutional capacity remains the precondition.

World Bank · Intergovernmental regional economic report

entry.title: Critical review finds Ghana's national AI strategy strong on readiness but thin on classroom detail
entry.summary:
A critical policy analysis by Matthew Nyaaba and nine co-authors develops an Education-Centred AI Policy Framework and applies it to Ghana's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for 2025 to 2035. The paper finds the strategy ambitious on AI literacy, youth skills and workforce readiness, but underdeveloped on teacher agency, pre-service teacher training, curriculum and assessment guidance, multilingual and culturally responsive pedagogy, and participatory governance at school level. The authors argue Ghana needs a sector-specific, education-centred AI implementation pathway that links workforce goals to teacher preparation, curriculum reform and learner protection.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 6 work on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the analysis is a useful reminder that national AI strategies across the Global South often outpace the classroom-level work needed to make them real for teachers and students.

arXiv preprint · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: US study finds no AI-driven unemployment spike yet for recent graduates
entry.summary:
A new National Bureau of Economic Research working paper by Robert Fairlie and Jane Wu examined United States employment data from June to August 2026 to test whether generative AI has begun to raise unemployment among recent university graduates. Comparing recent graduates with older graduates and with young people who did not go to university, the authors found no statistically significant summer 2026 rise in unemployment linked to artificial intelligence, although a broader measure that includes discouraged job seekers added nearly two percentage points to the recent-graduate rate.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 4 work on graduate capability, employability and just transitions, this is an early, data-based check on fears that generative AI is already destroying graduate jobs, a reminder to test local assumptions against evidence rather than headlines.

National Bureau of Economic Research · Economic research working paper

entry.title: Fort Hare study proposes Big Data framework to improve student retention in South Africa
entry.summary:
A new study in the South African Journal of Information Management, by Ganizani Mainoti and Roxanne Piderit of the University of Fort Hare, interviewed thirty academic staff at four public South African universities and reviewed their retention reports and policies. It found fragmented student data systems and limited data literacy among staff, and proposes a Big Data framework built on ethical data governance, integrated data processing, predictive analytics and personalised support to move universities from reacting to student drop-out towards preventing it.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 2 work on AI and predictive analytics for student success, retention and early warning, it is a home-grown, peer-reviewed case for the integrated data systems and governance that such analytics depend on.

University of Fort Hare, published in the South African Journal of Information Management · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: World Bank's 2026 World Development Report: AI needs reliable power, internet and skills to help developing countries
entry.summary:
The World Bank's World Development Report 2026, 'The Promise of Artificial Intelligence', sets out a strategy of adopt, adapt and advance for the 5.6 billion people living in low- and middle-income countries. It argues that developing countries do not need to build their own large AI models, but that importing AI tools alone will not help: artificial intelligence works best where infrastructure, including electricity and connectivity, and education systems are already reliable, and 'small AI' delivered by text message or basic phone can reach people where these are limited.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 6 work on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the report's warning that AI's benefits depend on reliable infrastructure and education systems, not just access to the technology, speaks directly to the conditions universities and governments across the Global South must still build.

World Bank · Intergovernmental flagship report

entry.title: UCT video: Cape Town summit brings the global debate on AI and universities to Africa
entry.summary:
In a video released ahead of the Times Higher Education World Academic Summit, the University of Cape Town said the gathering, co-hosted with the University of Bristol from 29 September to 1 October 2026, would be the first time it took place on the continent, bringing university leaders and policymakers together to debate artificial intelligence, the future of work, inequality and the purpose of universities. Vice-Chancellor Professor Mosa Moshabela said the summit was a chance for African universities to help shape the global agenda, reflecting his vision for UCT to advance teaching, research and societal impact while strengthening innovation and entrepreneurship for Africa, grounded in ubuntu.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 4 work on graduate capability, employability and just transitions, it is a reminder that African universities are now helping to set, not just follow, the global agenda on how higher education should respond to AI's effect on work and opportunity.

University of Cape Town (YouTube) · University video

entry.title: UNESCO working paper maps AI use across 200 Latin American and Caribbean universities

category.term: 19 countries, Latin America and the Caribbean

entry.summary:
A new UNESCO International Institute for Higher Education in Latin America and the Caribbean (IESALC) working paper, produced with the United Nations University Institute for the Advanced Study of Sustainability, maps how artificial intelligence is used across 200 higher education institutions in 19 Latin American and Caribbean countries, surveyed between August and October 2025. It looks across five dimensions, teaching and learning, research, community engagement, administration and governance, to show where AI is already in use, how it is governed, what institutional capacity exists and what gaps remain. The authors intend the findings to help institutional leaders and national policymakers integrate AI responsibly, ethically and inclusively.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 5 work on analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, it offers a rare region-wide evidence base on how universities govern and resource AI adoption, a comparison point for South Africa's own institutional policies.

UNESCO International Institute for Higher Education in Latin America and the Caribbean (IESALC), with UNU-IAS · Intergovernmental working paper

entry.title: MIT's own AI committee calls generative AI 'not an optional exercise' for teaching
entry.summary:
MIT's Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning and Research Training, charged by the Institute's leadership in January 2026, published its final report on 25 August 2026, describing generative AI as a force of extraordinary potential and disturbing risks that universities cannot treat as an optional policy exercise. Rather than one blanket rule, it recommends that departments and instructors set their own clear policies on when students must, may or must not use AI, redesign assessment and learning goals around it, and keep reviewing their approach as the technology changes. President Sally Kornbluth called the report a watershed moment, not only for MIT but for higher education generally.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 1 work on generative AI in higher education, a leading research university's own committee reaching this conclusion strengthens the case for Wits and its peers to treat course-level AI policy and assessment redesign as urgent, not optional.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology · University committee report

entry.title: New dashboard design principles aim to stop learning-analytics tools overstating what they can tell teachers
entry.summary:
Researchers presented TopoLA, a dashboard that applies a topological data-analysis method called zigzag persistent homology to learning-management-system data, to track how a class's learning activity changes over time. Because this analytical method has no settled rules for interpretation, the authors set out three design principles for any such dashboard: separate the raw measurement from its interpretation, reveal results in stages rather than all at once, and state the method's uncertainty openly rather than implying false precision.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 2 work on predictive and learning analytics for student success, it is a reminder that a dashboard which looks precise is not the same as one that is trustworthy, a distinction that matters for how early-warning and retention tools are designed and explained to the academics who rely on them.

arXiv (preprint, accepted at IADIS International Conference Information Systems 2026) · Peer-reviewed conference paper

entry.title: Study finds six AI chatbots give African computing students patchy, often Western-centric career advice

category.term: Ten African countries (study); United States (authors, Florida International University)

entry.summary:
Researchers at Florida International University tested six large language models, ChatGPT-4, DeepSeek, Gemini, Claude 3.5, Llama 3 and Mistral AI, on how well they described entry-level computing careers across ten African countries, analysing 60 responses against the Computing Curricula 2020 framework. The chatbots consistently covered technical skills such as cloud computing and programming, but averaged only 35.4 per cent for recognising local factors such as technology ecosystems, languages and national policy; the open-source Llama (4.47 out of 5) and DeepSeek (4.25) scored better on this than the proprietary ChatGPT-4 (3.90) and Claude (3.46), while the open-source Mistral AI scored 0.00 out of 4.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 4 work on graduate capability and employability, it is direct evidence that the AI career advice African students increasingly turn to can carry Western-centric assumptions about infrastructure and labour markets, which the authors argue calls for more contextual, Ubuntu-informed and human-guided approaches to career guidance in the Global South.

arXiv (preprint; submitted to Computers & Education Open) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Survey of 443 computing students finds the impostor phenomenon, not confidence, shapes how harshly they judge AI use as cheating
entry.summary:
A survey of 443 undergraduates in introductory and mid-level computing courses at a US university asked them to rate thirteen scenarios for how serious a case of cheating each was, alongside measures of self-efficacy and the impostor phenomenon. Students with a stronger impostor phenomenon were more likely to rate an AI-related scenario as serious cheating, while self-efficacy and the impostor phenomenon were themselves negatively correlated with one another.

Why it matters for AHEAD: It is useful evidence for Wits AHEAD's Pillar 1 work on generative AI and assessment integrity: how harshly a student judges AI use may say as much about their own confidence and sense of belonging as about the act itself, which matters for how academic integrity conversations and policies are framed.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Study of 30,000 student programming submissions finds AI-code matches rising over time, but says that alone cannot prove cheating
entry.summary:
A study of 29,970 student Python lab submissions from 2021, 2023 and 2025, compared against 90,000 solutions generated by three frontier large language models, finds that student code has increasingly come to resemble AI-generated solutions over time, including work that passed every hidden test. For tightly specified functions the models converged on only a few exact code structures, while open-ended tasks stayed diverse in both student and AI code. The authors conclude that such matches are useful for tracking population-level change in a class, but cannot by themselves show that one student used AI.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's Pillar 1 work on generative AI, assessment and integrity, it is a caution against using code-similarity matches as proof of individual misconduct, and a pointer towards redesigning assessment tasks and building reference solution banks instead of relying on detection alone.

arXiv (preprint, accepted Koli Calling 2026) · Working paper (arXiv preprint, accepted Koli Calling 2026)

entry.title: Wits and UJ researchers show early-warning systems for disengaged students are often tested unfairly
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of the Witwatersrand and the University of Johannesburg, in a preprint, show that early-warning systems for student disengagement are usually evaluated with information that would not actually have been available at the moment a prediction was made, making the systems look better than they would in real use. Testing three prediction methods on 49,329 weekly, real-time predictions drawn from Moodle learning-management-system logs, they found no single method won on every measure, and that lowering the alert threshold catches more at-risk students while raising the number of false alarms staff must act on.

Why it matters for AHEAD: It matters for Wits AHEAD's Pillar 2 work on predictive analytics for student success because it gives South African universities a more honest way to judge, before relying on it, whether an early-warning system will actually help catch disengaged students in time, not only how well it appears to work in hindsight.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Generative AI access does not mean equal use, study of Chinese, Japanese and Mongolian students finds
entry.summary:
A comparative study of 42 undergraduates, one university in each of China, Japan and Mongolia, finds that simply having access to generative AI tools does not make them equally useful for study. Researchers from the University of Osaka, the University of Minnesota, Waseda University and Kyoto University report that Chinese students moved between domestic and global AI systems, Japanese students mostly used global tools in Japanese, and Mongolian students often switched to English when Mongolian-language answers seemed weaker, while all three groups weighed accuracy, privacy, dependence and effects on their own thinking before trusting an answer.

Why it matters for AHEAD: It is a caution for Wits AHEAD's Pillar 1 work on generative AI in higher education: language and local technical conditions, not just access, decide whether generative AI genuinely helps students learn, a lesson that applies directly to multilingual, non-English-dominant university systems across the Global South.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Kyoto University framework offers universities a safer way to share student data with researchers
entry.summary:
Researchers at Kyoto University propose ReLEAF, a framework that lets universities and online learning platforms share the learning data they hold with outside researchers while better protecting student privacy. It gives researchers safely shareable synthetic data to explore first, then controlled access to real data only once a specific research need has been agreed with the institution that holds it. The design was shaped and tested through rounds of work with data custodians, researchers and students at Japanese universities.

Why it matters for AHEAD: It matters for Wits AHEAD's Pillar 5 work on analytics and data for education systems because many universities, including across the Global South, hold rich student data with no safe, agreed process for sharing it with researchers; this offers a practical template institutions could adapt.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: UNESCO opens global consultation on governing AI so that education remains a common good
entry.summary:
UNESCO has opened a global consultation, running to November 2026, inviting academics and policymakers to comment on a series of background papers on governing artificial intelligence in education. The lead paper, released ahead of Digital Learning Week 2026, sets out six ways education's purposes can be undermined when AI use goes ungoverned, and argues for treating education as a common good rather than leaving its governance to AI providers.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The consultation will shape UNESCO's guidance for ministries and universities, making it a reference point for Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, particularly for institutions in the Global South with less capacity to draft AI governance frameworks of their own.

UNESCO · Intergovernmental body, consultation paper

entry.title: Simple digital markers could flag at-risk first-year computer science students by week five, Southern African study finds
entry.summary:
Analysing four cohorts of first-year computer science students at a large public university in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers found that a weighted measure of academic momentum, combined with basic demographic data and simply whether a student had logged into the course's online learning system at all, correctly flagged 87 per cent of students who went on to fail. The authors argue the model is simple enough to run as an early-warning system from the fifth week of term.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A light-touch, low-data early-warning tool of this kind suits universities with limited institutional data infrastructure, directly advancing Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and predictive analytics for student success in under-resourced settings.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Nigerian study finds male pre-service STEM teachers report higher AI literacy than female peers
entry.summary:
A study of 541 pre-service STEM teachers at Lagos State University, published in the journal STEM Education, found relatively high self-reported AI literacy overall, with understanding of AI significantly predicting its use in teaching. It also found a statistically significant gender gap, with male trainee teachers reporting higher AI literacy than their female peers.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The gap matters for teacher-training programmes across the Global South that want AI literacy to spread evenly through the next generation of STEM teachers, a concern central to Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education.

STEM Education (AIMS Press) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Universities in Korea, Singapore and the United Kingdom take different paths to redesign teaching for AI

category.term: Korea, Singapore and the United Kingdom

entry.summary:
The Korea Times reports that Korean universities have added more than 4,000 places in AI and semiconductor-related fields since 2024 and that applications to AI departments at twenty major universities rose by 16% this year, while the government has had to cap new advanced-technology places at 434 for 2027 for want of staff and facilities. The same article contrasts this expansion with Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, which plans to fold AI into 40% of its undergraduate courses by 2030, and with King's College London and the London School of Economics, which are redesigning assessment and giving students and staff licensed access to AI tools rather than returning to handwritten exams.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, the comparison sets out two different responses to the same pressure, building more AI capacity or redesigning what and how students are assessed, a choice South African universities are weighing at the same time.

The Korea Times · Established national press, first instalment of a three-part series

entry.title: Study proposes voice-based AI interviews as a richer alternative to end-of-semester course surveys
entry.summary:
Researchers from the Technical University of Munich and the MIT Sloan School of Management propose replacing written end-of-semester course surveys with structured interviews conducted by a voice-based AI agent, which can ask follow-up questions where a written form cannot. A technical pilot at the Technical University of Munich found that telephone-based AI interviews are feasible, and the authors are now planning a full field study in an MIT Sloan course of about 60 students, scoring the feedback for specificity, thematic richness, constructive tone and contextual depth.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, the study points to a practical use for conversational AI inside teaching: turning a weak, low-response feedback loop into one detailed enough for lecturers and institutions to act on.

Technical University of Munich and the MIT Sloan School of Management, posted to arXiv · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Eduvos academic leader tells CNBC Africa that equal access to AI, not only AI literacy, will decide graduate employability
entry.summary:
At CNBC Africa's AI summit, an academic leader from the private higher education provider Eduvos said South African universities cannot wait to work out what artificial intelligence means for teaching and students, and that AI literacy, knowing when to lean on AI and when to reason independently, now matters as much as basic academic literacy. The leader warned that access to AI is not only access to a qualification: without digital support, infrastructure and devices for students from under-resourced backgrounds, AI could widen rather than narrow inequality among graduates entering the labour market.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the interview is a reminder that AI readiness in South African higher education depends as much on equitable access to tools and infrastructure as on teaching AI skills.

CNBC Africa · Broadcast interview, major African business channel

entry.title: Seven-country study finds universities at very different stages of AI readiness
entry.summary:
A seven-country study by WISE and the Institute of International Education finds universities at very different stages of generative AI readiness, with policy, student attitudes and infrastructure all uneven. At one private Ghanaian university 64% of faculty reported a clear AI policy, against 27% at a public research university, even though 89% of faculty across the study had already used AI themselves. The researchers warn that because leading AI models are trained mainly on English and other dominant languages, African and other Global South institutions risk staying consumers of AI rather than builders of it.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the study shows that readiness gaps between institutions, not only between countries, could widen rather than narrow inequality in how higher education adopts AI.

WISE and the Institute of International Education (IIE), reported by University World News · Established higher education press, reporting a WISE/IIE policy brief

entry.title: Dutch minister calls AI-written theses 'fraud', universities say detection scores cannot prove it
entry.summary:
A Dutch broadcaster's review of hundreds of recent master's theses at twelve universities found that in about one in five, chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini had contributed more text than the student had. Education minister Rianne Letschert called this 'fraud', but the universities' own body, Universiteiten van Nederland, said a detection score alone cannot prove misconduct and that the real question is how assessments are designed. Delft, Utrecht and Leiden have each restricted or banned AI detection tools on student work, arguing they are unreliable.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, the row shows how quickly an academic integrity dispute can turn political once a minister weighs in, and why the group argues for redesigning assessment rather than relying on detection software.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press

entry.title: Russell Group students say they are taught little about AI, Bett UK survey finds
entry.summary:
A Bett UK survey of more than 1,000 UK undergraduates finds that 77% of students at Russell Group universities say they are taught little or nothing about AI, against 64% at post-1992 universities. The same survey found 78% of students would welcome a technology-personalised degree that took less time to complete, while only 34% felt their university had been honest with them about realistic graduate outcomes. The Russell Group said its members are redesigning curricula and assessment rules in response.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, the finding that research-intensive universities teach AI skills less than other institutions do raises a direct equity question about which graduates enter an AI-shaped labour market prepared.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press

entry.title: New framework guides statistics and data science educators on teaching responsible generative AI use
entry.summary:
A team of statistics and data science educators has published a four part framework, covering understanding, development, reporting and safety, to guide how lecturers teach students to use generative AI tools responsibly in coding and statistical analysis. Refined through workshops and learner feedback, it has already been used in a massive open online course and in undergraduate and postgraduate teaching.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 3 (AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education) needs classroom ready frameworks, not only policy statements; this one gives Wits AHEAD a working model for teaching generative AI literacy inside a quantitative discipline.

arXiv · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: New tool scrambles assignment images so AI reading systems fail, but people can still read them
entry.summary:
Researchers have built AIRRI, a tool that reshapes the images of printed assignments using spacing, opacity and noise changes plus adversarial attacks, so that optical character recognition tools and AI chatbots struggle to transcribe them while a human reader still can. Tested against three reading systems, the strongest attack pushed one system's character error rate from 2.3% to 100% and another's word error rate from 24.9% to 96.7%. The team also released a dataset of higher education assignments to test the method.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 1 (generative AI in higher education: teaching, assessment, integrity) needs defences that work at the level of the assignment itself; Wits AHEAD watches tools like this test whether integrity can be engineered into course materials rather than policed after the fact.

arXiv · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: New framework argues the cost of AI essay-marking systems should be measured against trustworthy scores, not efficiency alone
entry.summary:
A new paper proposes a “Cost-Aware Measurement Design” framework for automated essay-scoring systems, arguing that the computing cost of AI marking is usually treated as a technical efficiency question when it is really a measurement-design choice. The framework defines a “cost per defensible score” that compares scoring systems only among designs meeting a minimum standard of trustworthy measurement, and treats an institution's governance and oversight capacity as a limit on which designs can be used at all, rather than as a price to be minimised away.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, the framework gives universities considering AI-assisted marking a concrete way to ask whether a cheaper system is actually producing defensible scores, rather than judging automated assessment tools on speed and cost alone.

arXiv (preprint) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: Study of a South African university finds online “participation profiles” mostly track how long a learner is observed, not how engaged they are
entry.summary:
Analysing 16,448 learner-course records from 4,599 students across 152 courses at a South African public university, researchers tested eight commonly used measures of online “participation” and found that all of them tracked how long a learner was observed in a course more closely than how actively the learner took part. After adjusting for this, a smaller set of measures still grouped learners into a broad two-profile pattern and a more detailed four-profile pattern, but only with moderate confidence.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and predictive analytics for student success, the finding is a direct caution for early-warning and retention systems built on South African data: unless the length of time a learner is tracked is accounted for, a learner flagged as “disengaged” may simply be one who was observed for less time, not one genuinely at risk.

entry.title: Study finds students who earn the same grade can have done very different amounts of their own thinking with AI help
entry.summary:
Analysing 150 recorded conversations between students and generative AI tools, a new study finds that students who direct the AI, integrate its output critically and evaluate it carefully can earn the same grade as students who let the AI do most of the thinking for them, so the final mark alone does not show how much of the work was genuinely the student's own. The author calls this gap “epistemic ownership” and argues that grading on output alone can reward very different levels of student engagement with the same score.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, the study strengthens the case for assessment that also looks at how a student used AI during a task, not only at the finished product, since two identical grades can hide very different learning.

entry.title: Wits tells top applicants AI should make graduates indispensable, not just employable
entry.summary:
More than 200 top-performing matriculants from Gauteng and further afield attended the Wits Vice-Chancellor's Top Applicants Event, where Wits alumnus Dr Craig Wing gave the keynote on artificial intelligence and the future world of work. Deputy Vice-Chancellor Professor Garth Stevens told the learners that university is a responsibility rather than only a route to employment, and that Wits wants its graduates to be more than employable: it wants them to be indispensable.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the event shows the University itself preparing incoming students for an AI-reshaped labour market from their first encounter with Wits, rather than leaving the question of employability until after graduation.

entry.title: Study finds AI grading tools miss most student misconceptions despite accurate scores
entry.summary:
A new study has examined whether large language models grading open-ended assignments in higher education are as useful as their accuracy scores suggest. Analysing 3,041 student responses to 50 open-ended computer science questions, scored by both human instructors and three commercial large language models, the researchers found that AI-generated feedback identified student misconceptions in only 5 to 7 per cent of cases, compared with 15 to 31 per cent for human teachers, and that AI feedback stayed uniformly positive regardless of answer quality. The study also found that AI-generated rubric sub-scores were so closely correlated with one another that they added little independent diagnostic information.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, the finding that AI grading can look accurate while missing most of the reasoning errors that matter for teaching is a caution against treating automated marking as a substitute for a teacher's diagnostic judgement.
